snip.t: History – bleeding / clotting: Easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, prolonged bleeding after minor cuts — Reduced synthesis of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and thrombocytopenia from splenic sequestration.
Bleeding / bruising: Easy bruising, petechiae, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, epistaxis, prolonged bleeding after minor cuts — Thrombocytopenia from marrow infiltration or peripheral consumption.
Bleeding gums, epistaxis: Thrombocytopenia + mucosal fragility.
Bleeding tendency (easy bruising, epistaxis): Thrombocytopenia from marrow infiltration; also platelet dysfunction from paraprotein.
Bleeding: epistaxis, gum bleed, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, intracranial haemorrhage (high mortality).
Site – mucosal (epistaxis, gum, menorrhagia), skin (petechiae, purpura), gastrointestinal, genitourinary, intracranial

qs.q: A 2-year-old boy has recurrent epistaxis and easy bruising. Bleeding time is prolonged, but PT and aPTT are normal. Platelet count is normal. Which defect best explains these findings?
o: Deficiency of factor VIII coagulant activity
Deficiency of factor IX coagulant activity
Impaired platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen
Excessive fibrinolysis due to plasminogen activation
Defective thrombin conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin
qs.e: Prolonged bleeding time with normal coagulation profile indicates a primary hemostasis defect like platelet adhesion issues.

qs.q: A 25-year-old male presents with progressive fatigue, pallor, and recurrent epistaxis. Laboratory workup reveals pancytopenia with a markedly hypocellular bone marrow biopsy containing mostly fat cells. Which pathogenetic mechanism is primarily responsible for his bone marrow failure?
o: Direct viral invasion of stromal elements inhibiting growth factor release
Malignant clonal expansion replacing normal marrow elements with blasts
Nutritional deficiency disrupting DNA synthesis and arresting cell maturation
Autoimmune cytotoxic T-cell attack directed against hematopoietic stem cells
Extracellular matrix fibrosis choking off sinusoidal vascular architecture
qs.e: Aplastic anemia is typically caused by an immune-mediated, T-cell-directed destruction of multipotent hematopoietic stem cells.

qs.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with pallor, fatigue, and recurrent epistaxis. Laboratory tests reveal pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow. Flow cytometry confirms a diagnosis of aplastic anemia. What is the primary cellular mechanism of this disease?
o: Infiltration of the marrow space by malignant clonal lymphoid cells.
Genetic mutation leading to accelerated red blood cell destruction.
Nutritional deficiency impairing nuclear DNA synthesis in precursors.
Autoimmune T-cell mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells.
Hypersplenism causing premature sequestration and clearance of cells.
qs.e: Acquired aplastic anemia is typically caused by autoreactive T-lymphocytes attacking and destroying hematopoietic stem cells.

qs.q: A 5-year-old child is evaluated for recurrent epistaxis and easy bruising. Laboratory results show a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with a normal prothrombin time (PT) and normal platelet count. Which clotting factor deficiency is most likely?
o: Inherited deficiency of coagulation factor VIII protein
Acquired reduction in functional plasma fibrinogen level
Congenital absence of vitamin K-dependent factor VII
Genetic impairment of circulating tissue factor pathway
Defective platelet membrane glycoprotein receptor complex
qs.e: Hemophilia A involves a deficiency of factor VIII, which prolongs the aPTT while leaving the PT and platelet count unaffected.

qs.q: An 8-year-old child presents with recurrent epistaxis and heavy bruising. Laboratory findings show a prolonged bleeding time, normal prothrombin time, and normal aPTT. Agglutination is absent when ristocetin is added to patient plasma. Which protein is deficient?
o: Plasma fibronectin acting as an adhesive bridge for vessels
Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex required for crosslinking
Coagulation factor XIII responsible for stabilization of clots
Von Willebrand factor mediating normal adhesion to subendothelium
Alpha-2 antiplasmin serving as a primary inhibitor of fibrinolysis
qs.e: Absent ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation alongside normal coagulation times points to a deficiency of von Willebrand factor.

qs.q: A 2-year-old boy presents with recurrent epistaxis and easy bruising. Platelet count is normal. PT is prolonged, PTT is normal. Mixing study corrects the PT. Which clotting factor is most likely deficient?
o: Deficiency in prothrombin, which is converted in the common pathway
Deficiency in factor VIII, which is part of the intrinsic pathway
Deficiency in factor X, which is common to both pathways
Deficiency in factor V, which is consumed in the final pathway
Deficiency in factor VII, which has the shortest half-life
qs.e: Isolated prolonged PT with normal PTT and correction on mixing indicates Factor VII deficiency.

qs.q: A 22-year-old female presents with recurrent episodes of epistaxis and heavy menstrual bleeding. Laboratory testing reveals a normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time, and reduced ristocetin cofactor activity. Which hemostatic protein is deficient?
o: Coagulation factor VIII required for intrinsic pathway propagation
Von Willebrand factor mediating platelet adhesion to subendothelium
Fibrinogen necessary for platelet cross-linking and clot stabilization
Tissue factor initiating the extrinsic coagulation cascade upon injury
Factor XIII responsible for covalent cross-linking of fibrin polymers
qs.e: Von Willebrand disease involves deficiency of vWF, which is required for platelet adhesion and factor VIII stabilization.

qs.q: A 10-year-old child presents with recurrent epistaxis and a nasal mass. Biopsy shows non-malignant tissue composed of fibrous stroma and numerous endothelium-lined vascular channels. What is the primary risk of biopsy?
o: Rapid malignant transformation of lesion
Massive hemorrhage from the vascular stroma
Complete airway obstruction via aspiration
Permanent anosmia from nerve damage
Severe local infection spreading to orbit
qs.e: Angiofibromas contain abundant thin-walled vessels lacking smooth muscle, predisposing to torrential bleeding.

es.q: A 65-year-old patient with a long-standing history of chronic Hepatitis C infection presents with progressive abdominal distension, disorientation, and spontaneous epistaxis. Discuss the most likely underlying chronic liver pathology, its pathogenesis, and comprehensively explain the clinical conseq
es.m: The most likely underlying chronic liver pathology in a patient with long-standing chronic Hepatitis C presenting with abdominal distension, disorientation, and epistaxis is **cirrhosis**. Hepatitis C is a known cause of macronodular cirrhosis. **Pathogenesis of Cirrhosis:** Cirrhosis is characterized by three key histological features: bridging fibrous septa (composed of collagen types I and III), disruption of the entire liver architecture, and parenchymal regenerative nodules. The key cell in the pathogenesis is the **Ito cell (hepatic stellate cell)**. ai.title: Epistaxis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Nosebleeds are common and usually benign, but can signal serious bleeding disorders or vascular disease. Assess severity, source, and underlying cause to guide urgent and definitive care.

sections.p: Epistaxis is bleeding from the nasal cavity, identified by visible blood from one or both nostrils. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and anterior nasal examination.
b: Confirm active bleeding vs. dried blood
Determine laterality and source (anterior vs. posterior)
Assess hemodynamic status (pulse, BP, capillary refill)

sections.p: Severity is staged by volume, duration, and hemodynamic impact. The common three‑tier system is used in low‑resource settings.
Causes are grouped by local, systemic, and iatrogenic factors. In East Africa, local trauma and infectious causes dominate.
b: Local trauma (nose picking, facial injury)
Dry climate / low humidity causing mucosal crusting
Infection: rhinosinusitis, malaria‑related thrombocytopenia
Systemic coagulopathy: vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, HIV‑related thrombocytopenia
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet use (e.g., aspirin, warfarin)
Herbal nasal preparations causing mucosal irritation

sections.p: Patients report sudden blood flow from one or both nostrils, often after a precipitating event. Posterior bleeds may present with blood in the oropharynx and coughing.
b: Bright red blood dripping from nostril(s)
Blood pooling in the nares or posterior pharynx
History of recent nose picking, trauma, or upper‑respiratory infection
Associated symptoms: dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath if volume is large

t.b: Detect anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukocytosis; low platelets suggest a systemic bleeding diathesis
Assess extrinsic pathway; prolonged PT indicates vitamin K deficiency or liver disease
Assess intrinsic pathway; prolonged aPTT points to hemophilia or lupus anticoagulant
Locate bleeding source; confirms posterior bleed when anterior packing fails
Identify hemodynamic compromise; hypotension mandates urgent fluid resuscitation

sections.p: Complications arise from uncontrolled bleeding, anemia, or underlying disease.
b: Persistent bleeding >30 minutes despite pressure
Systolic BP <90 mmHg or heart rate >120 bpm
Recurrent severe epistaxis (>3 episodes/year)
Signs of intracranial bleed (headache, vomiting, neurological deficit) after severe posterior bleed

sections.p: Initial steps focus on stabilisation, then local control, and finally treatment of the underlying cause.
b: Place patient upright, lean forward, apply firm pressure to Kiesselbach’s area for 10 minutes
If bleeding continues, use topical vasoconstrictor (e.g., oxymetazoline) – avoid in hypertension
Anterior packing with gauze or commercial tampon if pressure fails
Cauterisation (chemical with silver nitrate or electrical) of identified vessel
Posterior packing or balloon tamponade for posterior bleeds – requires ENT support
Treat systemic causes: vitamin K for deficiency, antiretroviral therapy for HIV‑related thrombocytopenia, stop anticoagulants if safe
Tranexamic acid (IV or topical) can be used when coagulation is impaired – avoid in active thromboembolism

sections.p: After control, address risk factors and arrange follow‑up to prevent recurrence.
b: Educate on gentle nasal hygiene, humidification, and avoiding nose picking
Review and adjust anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy
Screen for anemia or platelet disorders if recurrent
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and manage HIV to reduce coagulopathy

sections.p: Conditions that may mimic epistaxis or coexist.
b: Nasal foreign body causing bleeding
Nasal tumor (e.g., nasopharyngeal carcinoma) presenting with recurrent posterior bleed
Upper airway cough causing blood‑tinged sputum

sections.p: Lab values may be normal early or falsely altered by technical issues.
b: Platelet count can be falsely low if sample is delayed in a hot climate
PT/INR may be normal in early vitamin K deficiency; repeat after 12 hours if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Bleeding that does not stop after 30 minutes of firm pressure
Signs of shock (BP <90 mmHg, HR >120 bpm, altered mental status)

faq.q: Why is Kiesselbach’s area the most common source?
faq.a: It is a vascular anastomosis on the anterior septum where many small arteries converge, making it vulnerable to trauma and dryness.

faq.q: When should I consider a posterior bleed?
faq.a: If blood is seen in the posterior pharynx, the patient coughs up blood, or anterior packing fails, suspect posterior epistaxis.

faq.q: Can I use nasal decongestant sprays long term to prevent epistaxis?
faq.a: Short‑term use helps control bleeding, but chronic use can cause rebound congestion and mucosal atrophy, increasing bleed risk.

exam: A 12‑year‑old presents with 20 minutes of unilateral bleeding after nose picking – what is your immediate management? — Apply firm pressure to Kiesselbach’s area for 10 minutes, use topical vasoconstrictor, and assess hemodynamics.

A patient on warfarin has a posterior bleed that persists despite anterior packing – what next step? — Arrange posterior packing or balloon tamponade and reverse anticoagulation if INR >3, after weighing thrombotic risk.
How does HIV‑related thrombocytopenia change your approach to epistaxis? — Expect low platelets, obtain CBC, consider tranexamic acid, and coordinate with HIV care for ART optimization.

What clinical feature distinguishes an anterior from a posterior epistaxis? — Posterior bleeds produce blood in the oropharynx and may cause coughing, while anterior bleeds are visible at the nostril.
Why is silver nitrate cautery contraindicated on a septal perforation? — It can enlarge the perforation and cause further bleeding; avoid if perforation is present.

A patient with chronic rhinosinusitis and frequent bleeds is found to have a low vitamin K level – what is the rationale for giving vitamin K? — Vitamin K restores synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, correcting the coagulopathy that predisposes to bleeding.

Explain why tranexamic acid is useful in epistaxis but should be avoided in a patient with recent deep‑vein thrombosis. — It inhibits fibrinolysis, stabilising clots, but may increase thrombotic risk in patients with active clotting disorders.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt you to order a head CT in a patient with epistaxis? — New onset severe headache, vomiting, or focal neurological deficit suggesting intracranial hemorrhage.
